old.text: Abstract

new.text: Abstract

old.text: Systematic characterization of gesture stimuli is important for vocabulary-learning research, but human annotation is slow and costly to scale. Video-language models (VLMs) may support this process, yet their correspondence with human judgment requires empirical evaluation. We benchmarked eleven configurations from three model families (Google Gemini, OpenAI GPT, Alibaba Qwen) against 230 human raters across four language cohorts, who rated 148 instructional gesture videos on seven dimensions drawn from the Gesture Memory Support Model. Mean absolute error across configurations ranged from 0.53 to 1.12 points on five-point scales, and pooled rank correlations ranged from .62 to .69. Crucially, error and rank-order agreement dissociated: dimensions with the lowest error (enactment potential, motional salience) had the weakest or even negative rank correlations, while iconicity showed the opposite pattern. This dissociation mirrored a structural feature of the human data itself, where the same two dimensions showed the lowest interrater reliability and most compressed rating distributions. Models reliably rated mismatched gesture–word pairs lower than matched pairs, indicating genuine sensitivity to semantic compatibility, though residual ratings remained above the human floor. Cultural familiarity showed the largest model–human discrepancies; independently, human ratings on this and related dimensions varied systematically by language cohort even after controlling for item identity, indicating that the human reference itself is not culturally neutral. These findings support selective, dimension-specific use of VLMs for gesture annotation under human oversight, rather than uniform deployment across the full rating profile. The benchmark establishes correspondence with human judgment; it does not establish whether model- or human-derived ratings predict vocabulary-learning outcomes, which remains an open empirical question.

old.text: Introduction

new.text: Introduction

old.text: Gesture has long been recognized as a powerful facilitator of language learning and memory. In second language (L2) acquisition research, a substantial body of behavioral, cognitive, and neuroscientific evidence has demonstrated that gestures enrich lexical encoding, strengthen semantic associations, and improve long-term retention (Macedonia, 2025). Instructional gestures, movements deliberately paired with words, may depict a word’s meaning, such as raising an imaginary cup to the mouth when learning the L2 word for “to drink,“ or establish an arbitrary association with it; mnemonic benefits have been shown for both concrete and abstract vocabulary (Macedonia & Knösche, 2011). From a neuroscientific perspective, gesture-supported learning engages distributed neural networks linking word representations with sensory and motor information (Macedonia et al., 2011; Macedonia & Mueller, 2016; Macedonia et al., 2019; Mayer et al., 2017), consistent with broader theories of embodied cognition proposing that conceptual knowledge is grounded in sensorimotor experience (Barsalou, 2008). A recent three-level meta-analysis of 52 studies and 442 effect sizes further supports the educational relevance of embodied vocabulary instruction (X. Li et al., 2026).

old.text: A significant methodological bottleneck constrains this purpose: operationalizing gesture-related variables typically requires expert human annotation of video data, with each gesture rated independently across seven dimensions under clearly defined criteria. This process is time-consuming, costly, and inherently subjective, and inter-rater agreement becomes increasingly difficult to maintain as stimulus sets grow or additional linguistic populations are included. Ratings may also reflect raters’ own linguistic experience and cultural familiarity, meaning human annotation provides a population-dependent reference rather than an error-free standard. As gesture datasets expand, reliance on manual coding becomes increasingly impractical for large-scale or longitudinal research, creating a clear need for computational methods capable of estimating gesture-related covariates reliably and reproducibly.

old.text: The rapid emergence of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) offers a promising avenue for addressing this bottleneck. Advances in multimodal artificial intelligence have produced models capable of jointly processing visual, temporal, and linguistic information, enabling forms of video understanding and semantic reasoning that go beyond earlier pipelines reliant on low-level motion tracking or pose estimation. Extending the existing use of AI-generated psycholinguistic ratings (e.g., word concreteness, familiarity) to gesture stimuli introduces additional demands: models must track movement over time, evaluate relationships between visible actions and intended lexical meaning, and interpret dimensions, such as cultural familiarity, whose relevance may itself vary across contexts. Whether VLMs can meet these demands well enough to generate useful, GMSM-aligned covariates is an open empirical question.

We evaluate both zero-shot prompting and the potential for fine-tuned, gesture-specialized architectures. Because agreement between models alone cannot establish correspondence with human raters, and because an aggregate performance measure may conceal dimension-specific differences, evaluation must distinguish rank-order association, absolute agreement, and systematic bias—distinctions essential for identifying which model-generated ratings are suitable for downstream statistical use and which still require human oversight. old.text: 2.1.1 Iconicity

new.text: 2.1.1 Iconicity

old.text: Iconicity concerns the extent to which a gesture’s form or movement resembles aspects of its intended lexical meaning. For example, outlining a roof with the hands can depict a perceptual feature associated with house, whereas miming drinking can represent an action associated with to drink. Iconicity is thus evaluated for a particular gesture–meaning pairing rather than inferred from a broad gesture category. Different representational strategies can produce similarly transparent relationships between movement and meaning (Dingemanse et al., 2020; Perniss et al., 2010; Perniss & Vigliocco, 2014). Research comparing semantically congruent and incongruent gesture–word pairings supports the importance of this relationship. Congruent gestures can facilitate vocabulary learning, whereas conflicting gestural information can interfere with encoding and semantic processing (Kelly et al., 2010; Macedonia et al., 2011). However, resemblance is not a prerequisite for mnemonic support. Consistently paired arbitrary gestures can also facilitate learning despite lacking a transparent resemblance to the referent (Huang et al., 2019; Macedonia & Knösche, 2011). A low iconicity rating therefore does not establish that a gesture is ineffective. Moreover, an arbitrary but stable association must be distinguished from an unrelated movement that varies across presentations and provides no consistent retrieval cue.

old.text: 2.1.3 Motional salience

new.text: 2.1.3 Motional salience

old.text: Motional salience concerns the perceptual prominence of a gesture’s movement dynamics. Relevant characteristics include spatial extent, vigor, abruptness, and other features that make movement conspicuous. The proposed link with learning is attentional: perceptually prominent movements may increase the likelihood that gestural information is noticed and encoded. This dimension is related to bodily and motoric engagement in existing embodied-learning frameworks (Johnson-Glenberg et al., 2014; Skulmowski & Rey, 2018), but it specifically characterizes the movement presented to the learner. A learner can observe a highly salient movement without reproducing it. Motional salience also differs from emotional expression. A large movement can be emotionally neutral, while a subtle movement can convey strong affective information. Macedonia and Klimesch’s (2014) gesture for seal, involving simulated balancing of a ball on the nose, illustrates how dynamic movement and playful affect may coexist. However, the memorability of this item cannot establish an independent effect of motional salience because movement, affective associations, and lexical characteristics were not isolated. The GMSM makes these potentially overlapping properties explicit so that their contributions can subsequently be examined.

The relevant property is therefore emotional compatibility rather than intensity alone. A neutral expression may be appropriate for an emotionally neutral action, whereas an expression of fear may contribute relevant information when representing afraid. These findings motivate the dimension but do not directly validate emotional salience fit as a predictor of L2 vocabulary learning. Within the GMSM, facial expression contributes to this dimension insofar as it supplies relevant affective information; facial expressiveness is not a separate dimension or an equivalent measure.

old.text: 2.1.5 Gesture complexity fit

new.text: 2.1.5 Gesture complexity fit

old.text: Gesture complexity fit describes whether a gesture’s motoric complexity is appropriate for its target meaning, learner population, and instructional mode. Observable complexity includes the number and sequence of movement phases, the involvement of different body segments, and precision and coordination requirements. For example, to go may be represented by walking in place or by moving two fingers to depict walking legs. Both gestures can represent the intended meaning while differing in motor demands. The theoretical rationale draws on cognitive load theory, particularly the dependence of processing demands on interacting task elements and learners’ prior knowledge (Chen et al., 2023; Paas & Sweller, 2012; Sweller, 1988). Motoric complexity should nevertheless not be equated with cognitive load: a familiar action involving several movements may be easier to interpret than a physically simple but ambiguous gesture. Evidence that gesture can reduce processing demands in some contexts while introducing additional demands in others supports this context-sensitive approach (Cook et al., 2012; Goldin-Meadow et al., 2001; Post et al., 2013). High complexity fit consequently means that the movement’s demands are appropriate, not that the gesture is maximally simple.

new.text: 2.1.6 Cultural familiarity

old.text: Cultural familiarity describes how recognizable and interpretable a gesture is within a specified learner population’s sociocultural repertoire. Gesture meanings and conventions vary across communities, making familiarity dependent on experience rather than a universally fixed property of movement (Kita, 2009). Research has shown that culturally familiar gestures can influence speech perception and that observing culture-specific gestures can differentially engage the motor system (Billot-Vasquez et al., 2020; Molnar-Szakacs et al., 2007). These findings support the relevance of cultural experience to gesture processing without directly establishing its contribution to vocabulary retention. Cultural familiarity must be distinguished from both iconicity and semantic congruence. A gesture may depict a referent transparently without being conventional in a particular community. Conversely, a familiar emblem may have little resemblance to its meaning, or may conflict with the word accompanying it. Ratings of cultural familiarity therefore require an explicit reference population. This requirement is particularly relevant when comparing human judgments across linguistic cohorts or evaluating model ratings that may reflect unspecified cultural assumptions.

old.text: 2.1.7 Enactment potential

new.text: 2.1.7 Enactment potential

old.text: Enactment potential concerns how readily a specified learner population could reproduce a gesture accurately under defined instructional conditions. Its theoretical relevance derives partly from research on the enactment effect: performing actions during encoding can improve memory for associated verbal material relative to verbal encoding alone (Bäckman & Nilsson, 1985; Cohen, 1981; Engelkamp & Zimmer, 1989). Accounts of this effect emphasize the integration of verbal, motor, and proprioceptive information, which may provide additional retrieval routes (Zimmer, 2001). A systematic review and meta-analysis confirms substantial enactment benefits while documenting variation across tasks and comparison conditions (Roberts et al., 2022). The GMSM distinguishes enactment potential from both actual gesture production and the resulting memory benefit. A gesture can be easy to reproduce even when learners only observe it, and ease of reproduction does not establish that performing it improves learning. Enactment potential also differs from complexity fit: the former concerns reproducibility, whereas the latter concerns whether the movement’s complexity is appropriate for its instructional purpose. Their overlap and separate contributions remain empirical questions.

old.text: 2.2 Computational Approaches to Gesture Analysis

new.text: 2.2 Computational Approaches to Gesture Analysis

old.text: The increasing availability of multimodal learning datasets has stimulated growing interest in computational approaches to gesture analysis. old.text: Several extensions follow directly from the limitations above. A reliability study, repeating inference on the same items across multiple runs, prompt paraphrases, and, where available, temperature or sampling settings, would establish whether VLM ratings are stable enough to trust a single pass, which the present design cannot determine. A direct zero-shot-versus-fine-tuned comparison, using the same stimulus set and evaluation pipeline reported here, would directly address RQ4/H4, which remains open. Because cultural familiarity and several other dimensions proved population-dependent even in the human data, a deliberately cross-cultural validation design, sampling comparable numbers of raters and, ideally, comparable model prompts per language/cultural cohort — would help separate genuine model limitations from reference-target instability. A revised control-item design, in which the same gestures are evaluated under both a matched and a mismatched target word, would also let future work isolate semantic-compatibility effects from item-composition effects. Most importantly, connecting GMSM dimension scores, whether human- or model-generated, to actual vocabulary-learning outcomes in a controlled instructional study is the necessary next step before any claim about the predictive or practical value of automated gesture annotation can be made. Finally, expanding the stimulus set, refining the operational definitions to more closely track the current GMSM, and formally identifying which items function as mismatched controls in the shared data would together allow tighter confidence intervals around the dimension-specific correlations reported here and let future benchmarks track improvement in specific, currently weak dimensions such as cultural familiarity and facial-expression salience.

old.text: 8. Conclusion

new.text: 8. Conclusion

old.text: The methodological bottleneck motivating this study, that gesture characterization from video is slow, costly, and difficult to scale, remains real, and video-language models offer a partial, not a complete, solution to it. Across seven GMSM-aligned dimensions, model-generated ratings showed genuine but uneven correspondence with human judgment: consistently useful for visually transparent dimensions like iconicity and sensorimotor imagery, and not yet trustworthy for population-dependent dimensions like cultural familiarity or facial-expression salience, where errors approached or exceeded a full scale point and where the human reference itself proved unstable across language cohorts. Absolute error, systematic bias, and within-dimension ranking provided complementary rather than redundant information, and did not consistently favor the same configurations — underscoring that this benchmark establishes descriptive correspondence with human judgment, not predictive validity for learning outcomes. The most actionable conclusion is therefore not “VLMs work” or “VLMs don’t work,” but that automated gesture annotation should be deployed selectively, dimension by dimension, with explicit human review retained for the dimensions and item types, near-midpoint ratings, culturally specific items, mismatched pairings, where both this study’s human and model data agree that disagreement is highest. Used this way, VLMs can plausibly extend, rather than replace, the human annotation pipeline that gesture-supported vocabulary research currently depends on, while the predictive value of these gesture profiles for vocabulary learning itself remains to be tested empirically.
